newsitem.title: CANADA: McDonough call for FX stability falls on deaf ears.
newsitem.headline: McDonough call for FX stability falls on deaf ears.

text.p: Volatility-hungry foreign exchange dealers cringed on Friday as New York Federal Reserve President William McDonough called for more transparency and greater stability in currency markets.
Currency volatility -- which provides greater trading and profit opportunities for dealers -- has been on the decline in recent years, sapping foreign exchange desks of a vital income source.

"Volatility is the bread and butter for traders and banks themselves," said Theo van Koningsveld, a senior vice president at Rabobank International, based in the Netherlands, "In reality traders are eager for any volatility in any currency they can find."

But McDonough, speaking to an audience of unreceptive currency dealers at the 39th annual congress of the Association Cambiste Internationale, said lower volatility was actually in the long-term interests of the industry.

"Excess volatility can diminish resources otherwise allocated to productive growth," said McDonough. "I am persuaded that what is good for economic growth is good for financial markets and the individuals who participate in these markets."

So far in 1997, market fluctuations have been unusually wild. The dollar accelerated to a four-and-a-half year high against the yen and a three-year peak against the mark roughly one month ago, before succumbing to a heavy bout of selling and retreating over ten percent against the Japanese currency to a recent low of 111.98 yen.
This has cheered an industry which just six months ago was suffering in the wake of a prolonged period of relative market stability.

"What he wants to cut out are the radical moves that have happened in the past and that are happening less and less now," said Dudley Hoskin, an executive in the foreign exchange and capital markets division at Macquarie Bank Ltd in Sydney, Australia.

But for traders, who have converged on Toronto amid talk of further industry consolidation in the run-up to European economic and monetary union, McDonough's calls for stability were less than welcome.
"The idea is to make money and the more volatility the more opportunity there is for that," said Paul Delamain, a dealer with Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
